COUNSEL:

William Henkel, Esq., Q.C. and Ms. I. Freund,
for the Appellant

Timothy J. Boyle, Esq., for the Respondent

T.W. Wakeling, Esq., for London Drugs Ltd.
and The Seventh Day Adventist Church in Canada

Julius Isaac, Esq., Q.C. and R. MacDonald,
Esq., for the Attorney General of Canada

REASONS FOR
JUDGMENT

OF THE HONOURABLE MR JUSTICE LAYCRAFT

[
1
]

The issues on this appeal are whether The Lord's
Day Act is
ultra vires
the Parliament of Canada, or if it is not,
whether it is inconsistent with The
Charter of Rights
and Freedoms and
therefore of no force and effect.

[
2
]

On Sunday, May 30, 1982 officers of the Calgary
City Police attended at the Respondent's retail store and watched clerks sell
groceries, plastic cups and a bicycle padlock. The Respondent was charged with
an offence against Section 4 of The Lord's Day Act (R.S.C. 1970, Ch. L-13) and
the Attorney General of Alberta granted his fiat for the prosecution. On March
9, 1982 in lengthy Reasons for Judgment, His Honour Judge Stevenson acquitted
the Respondent in Provincial Court on two grounds which I summarize as follows:

1.      Though the courts have long held The
Lord's Day Act to be a valid exercise by Parliament of the federal power oyer
criminal law, that conclusion was based upon the incorrect premise that
Christianity was once part of the common law. Even assuming that premise was
correct, it is no longer valid because social conditions and public perceptions
have changed. He held further that if Christianity ever was part of the common
law, the
Charter of Rights
effected a change in the common law. In the result,
The Lord's Day Act is, he held, no longer to be justified under the criminal
law power and is
ultra vires
the Parliament of Canada.

2.     In any event The Lord's Day Act breaches
the fundamental freedom of conscience and religion guaranteed by
Section 2
of
the
Charter of Rights
enacted in The Constitution Act 1982 (U.K. Ch II). It
cannot be justified under Section 1 as a reasonable limitation of a fundamental
freedom in a free and democratic society. Being inconsistent with the Charter
of Rights, it is of no force and effect.

[
3
]

The Alberta Crown, as the prosecutor of the
charge, has appealed the acquittal and the Attorney General of Canada has intervened
in support of Alberta. In addition, on application, the Court permitted two
interventions in support of the acquittal by The Seventh Day Adventist Church
in Canada and by London Drugs Ltd. The latter company was one of 29 different
bodies corporate which were subjected to similar prosecutions in Edmonton and
acquitted in Provincial Court by His Honour, Judge Jones. He declined to follow
the decision of Judge Stevenson on the first ground summarized above but
reached the same conclusion that The Lord's Day Act is inconsistent with The

Charter of Rights
.

I

Is The Lord's
Day Act Ultra Vires the Parliament of Canada?

[
4
]

For more than thirty years after Confederation
the only legislation restricting activities on Sunday was enacted by the
provinces. The Ontario statute
"An Act to Prevent the Profanation of
the Lord's Day
" R.S.O.
1897, Ch. 246
, which had existed even prior to
Confederation is an example. In 1903 in
Attorney General for Ontario v.
Hamilton Street Railway Co.
(1903)
1903 CanLII 121 (UK JCPC)
, A.C. 524 the Privy Council held this
statute to be beyond provincial powers as an intrusion into the federal field
of criminal law.

[
5
]

The decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada
have since that time continued to characterize Lord's Day observance
legislation as criminal law. In
The Sunday Laws Reference
(1905)
1905 CanLII 54 (SCC)
, 35
S.C.R. 581, the Court followed the
Hamilton Street Railway
case (supra)
in holding that proposed legislation to prohibit on Sunday the performance of
work and labour, the transaction of business, engaging in sport for gain or keeping
open places of entertainment, was within the jurisdiction of Parliament as part
of the criminal law.

[
6
]

In
Ouimet v. Bazin
(1912)
1912 CanLII 628 (SCC)
, 46 S.C.R. 502
the court held invalid Quebec legislation relating to Sunday as being within
the exclusive authority of Parliament. At Page 507 Fitzpatrick, C.J. said:

"It appears to me on the whole
abundantly clear that the intention of the legislature was to forbid certain
things which, in its opinion, are calculated to interfere with the proper
observance of Sunday. In the
Hamilton Street Railway
case their
Lordships hold, impliedly at least, that Christianity is part of the common law
of the realm; that the observance of the Sabbath is a religious duty; and that
a law which forbids any interference with that observance is, in its nature,
criminal …

It is impossible for me to believe that
the legislature intended by the enactment in question, to regulate civil
rights. On the contrary, the evident object was to conserve public morality and
to provide for the peace and order of the public on the Lord's Day. I am
confirmed in this belief by the title of the Act which is described as 'A law
concerning the observance of Sunday'; … "

At page 525, Duff, J. (as he then was) said:

"The Quebec statute which is
impeached on this appeal professes to create offences which, in my opinion, if
validly created would be offences against the criminal law within the meaning
of section 91, sub-section 27, of the 'British North America Act'. The
enactment appears to me, in effect, to treat the acts prohibited as
constituting a profanation of the Christian institution of the Lord's Day and
to declare them punishable as such. Such an enactment we are, in my opinion,
bound to hold, on the authority of
The Attorney General
v.
Hamilton
Street Railway Co.
, to be an enactment dealing with the subject of the
criminal law."

[
7
]

Again in
Henry Birks & Sons v. Montreal
and Attorney General of Quebec

1955 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1955] S.C.R. 799, Quebec legislation
forcing businesses to close on certain Roman Catholic religious holidays was found
to be invalid because it infringed on the criminal law powers of Parliament. At
page 807 Fauteux, J. said:

"On ne dispute plus gu'une législation
sur 1'observance du dimanche fait partie du droit criminel au Canada comme en Angleterre
et est, comme telle, en notre pays, de la competénce exclusive du Parlement."

[
8
]

In
Robertson and Rosetanni v. The Queen

1963 CanLII 17 (SCC)
, [1963] S.C.R. 651 to which I will refer again in relation to the
Charter of
Rights
, it was taken to be beyond question that The Lord's Day Act was within the
distribution of legislative powers given to the federal government. Similarly
in 1978 in
The Corporation of the City of Hamilton v. The Canadian Transport
Commission

1977 CanLII 28 (SCC)
, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 640 at 642-643, Martland, J. said, referring to
The
Lord's Day Act:

"It is necessary to consider the Act
as a whole in order to make that determination. Its general purpose is to
maintain Sunday observance, and it is because of that that its constitutional
validity has been supported as being legislation in relation to criminal law
under
s. 91(27)
of the
British North America Act, 1867
.
That purpose is,
however, sought to be achieved by preventing the transaction of business, the
pursuing of a gainful calling, or the employment of any person to do work,
business or labour on a Sunday."

[
9
]

In his Reasons for Judgment, Judge Stevenson
analyzed a number of authorities and summarized his conclusions in these terms:

"I find, firstly, in Canada,
following Confederation in 1867, it was generally believed that legislative
authority over Sunday observance was committed to the Provincial legislatures
under Section 92.

Secondly, this situation was changed by
the Hamilton Street Railway Reference in 1902, when the Judicial Committee held
that Sunday observance legislation was 'criminal law in its widest sense'.

Three, Courts in Canada have religiously
followed the Hamilton Street Railway ratio to the present day, with the
exception of Mr. Justice Riley in the 1972 Alberta Boardwalk Merchandise Mart
Ltd. case (
R. v. Boardwalk Merchandise Mart Ltd.

1972 CanLII 1264 (AB SCTD)
, [1972] 6 W.W.R. 1).

Four, the scope of the definition of the
criminal law power as set out in the Hamilton Street Railway case, has been
substantially narrowed in Canada.

Five, there is serious doubt that
Christianity was ever part of the common law of the realm.

Six, adoption of this precept in
subsequent decisions may, as a result, bring their conclusions into question.

Seventh, even if Christianity was at one
time part of the common law of the realm, its influence on the criminal law has
been virtually eliminated by changed social conditions and attitudes and by
statute.

Eight, without the moral grounds that the
common law may have provided, there is no public purpose, nor is there any evil
or menace to suppress. Therefore, there can no longer be any valid reason for
the Lord's Day Act to be upheld as valid criminal law. In short, as Mr. Justice
Riley held in the Boardwalk Merchandise Mart Ltd. case at Page 20:

'It is deprived of its constitutional
underpinnings.'

I hold that the Lord's Day Act is ultra vires
the Parliament of Canada."

[
10
]

The statement by Judge Stevenson in his seventh
reason that the common law has been varied "by statute" apparently
refers to his earlier conclusion that the
Charter of Rights
amended the common
law and so removed Sunday observance legislation from the federal jurisdiction
under criminal law. He reached this conclusion by noting that the preamble to
the Charter of Rights recognizes the existence of God but does not
"specify a Christian God, nor does the Charter recognize Canada as a
Christian nation". In my view, however, the Charter did not intend to
effect a redistribution of legislative powers in Canada. Indeed, Section 31 of
the Charter expressly so provides: "Nothing in this Charter extends the
legislative powers of any body or authority". Moreover, Section 33
provides that Parliament or a Legislature may override the Charter. Thus if a
legislative power had been transferred by the Charter either Parliament or a
provincial legislature could retransfer it by its unilateral action. That would
be an odd result of enactment of the Charter. In my view the Charter of Rights
did not remove Sunday observance legislation from the field of criminal law.

[
11
]

In reaching his eight conclusions, Judge
Stevenson followed and quoted extensively from the judgment of Riley, J. in
R.
v. Boardwalk Merchandise Mart Ltd.
(supra). When that case came on appeal
to this Court (
1972 CanLII 983 (AB SCAD)
, [1973] 1 W.W.R. 190) the appeal was allowed without calling on
the Crown. McDermid, J.A., for the Court, reviewed those of the cases to which
I have referred above which had then been decided. He concluded that this Court
was bound on principles of
stare decisis
to hold that Sunday observance
legislation is within the federal powers reserved under Section 91(27) of The
British North America Act and so comes under the exclusive authority of
Parliament. Leave to appeal from this decison to the Supreme Court of Canada
was refused.

[
12
]

In 1977 in
Corporation of the City of
Hamilton v. The Canadian Transport Commission
(supra) the Supreme Court of
Canada was again unanimous in its characterization of The Lord's Day Act as
criminal law. Even assuming for the purpose of argument that changing public
perceptions or attitudes could render
ultra vires
, a statute found
repeatedly by the Courts over three-quarters of a century to be within federal
powers, nothing demonstrates the profound change in public attitudes in the
last six years which would be required to warrant the conclusion reached. In my
opinion The Lord's Day Act is valid federal legislation under the criminal law
power specified in Section 91(27) of The British North America Act.

II

The
Charter of Rights

[
13
]

The two basic questions under The
Charter of
Rights
argued on this appeal were whether The Lord's Day Act breaches the
fundamental freedom of conscience and religion under Section 2 and, if so,
whether the Act is nevertheless within the limitation on fundamental freedoms
specified by Section 1 as being "demonstrably justified in a free and
democratic society". Two preliminary points were argued, however, on
behalf of the two Attorneys General. It was urged that:

1.     A corporation
does not have rights under the
Charter
and in particular it is not given the
fundamental freedom of conscience and religion under
Section 2
or any right to
apply to a Court under Section 24.

2.     In any event
the Provincial Court of Alberta is not "a court of competent
jurisdiction" under Section 24. Thus it is said that a person charged with
crime in that Court may not rely on the
Charter
in his defence.

[
14
]

I shall consider these preliminary points
together. In my view to accede to the rigid interpretation of the
Charter
urged
by the Attorneys General would deprive Canadians of the full measure of rights
and freedoms the Charter was intended to guarantee.

[
15
]

Writing twenty years ago in his text
The
Commerce Power in Canada and the United States
Professor Alex. Smith
enjoined judges to bring to the exposition and interpretation of constitutional
documents, not a restricted legalistic approach but, "the genius of
statecraft". Many other eloquent statements also bear witness to the
special position in judicial interpretation of constitutional provisions. In
Re
Southam Inc. and the Queen
(1983)
1983 CanLII 1707 (ON CA)
, 3 CCC (3d) 515 MacKinnon, A.C.J.O.
referred to Lord Sankey's "living tree" (
Edwards v. Attorney
General of Canada

1929 CanLII 438 (UK JCPC)
, [1930] A.C. 124 at 136) and said at page 524:

"The spirit of this new 'living
tree' planted in friendly Canadian soil should not be stultified by narrow
technical, literal interpretations without regard to its background and purpose;
capability for growth must be recognized."

[
16
]

In
Minister of Home Affairs v. Fisher
[1979]
3 All E.R. 21
, Lord Wilberforce giving a decision of the Privy Council
relating to the Bermudan constitution referred to "the broad and ample
style of its draftsmanship". He also noted the influence on most modern
constitutions of the European Convention for the Protection
of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms and of the United Nations Universal
Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. He said at page 25:

"These antecedents, and the form of
Chapter I itself, call for a generous interpretation avoiding what has been
called 'the austerity of tabulated legalism', suitable to give to individuals
the full measure of the fundamental rights and freedoms referred to."

[
17
]

There can be no question that these principles
must govern the exposition of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
by
the Canadian courts and that Canadian judges, too, must avoid "the
austerity of tabulated legalism".

[
18
]

This Court has not previously been required to
consider whether the position of a corporation is different under the
Charter
of Rights
than that of any other person. In
Southam v. Director of
Investigation and Research of the Combines Investigation Branch
(1983)
1983 ABCA 32 (CanLII)
, 24
Alta L.R. (2d) 307 (Alta. C.A.) where a corporation argued the invalidity of
the search and seizure powers under The Combines Act, the federal Crown
expressly declined to argue the point.

[
19
]

A complication in interpreting the
Charter
is
the different terminology used in it to specify to whom it applies.
"Everyone" is the term used in
Sections 2
, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12 and 17.
Referring to voting rights and mobility rights in Sections 3 and 6 the words
are "every citizen". In Section 11 which expounds the rights of those
charged with an offence, the term is "any person". Section 15 which
grants equality before the law (and which comes into force on April 17, 1985)
uses "every individual". Section 19, dealing with language rights
uses "any person". Section 24 uses "anyone".

[
20
]

"Everyone" is a word of wide import.
Both the
Shorter Oxford Dictionary
and the
Random House Dictionary

give meanings for "everyone" and "everybody" which show the
words are synonymous. They are of wider import than the word "person"
but include it. Similarly, "anyone" is shown to be synonymous with
"any person".

[
21
]

The Canada Act 1982 incorporating the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
is, of course, a statute of the Parliament of
the United Kingdom. If any interpretation act is to be applied to the Charter
it would be that of the United Kingdom enacted as 1978 (Eng.) C. 30, Sched. 1.
It defines the word person as including "a body of persons corporate or
incorporate". Apart from statutory interpretation acts, however, it has
been held that the word "person" in a public statute includes a
corporation. In
Union Colliery Co. v. The Queen
(1900)
1900 CanLII 31 (SCC)
, 31 S.C.R. 81 at
pages 88-89, Sedgewick, J. said:

" 'Everyone' is an expression of the
same kind as person, and therefore includes bodies corporate unless the context
requires otherwise. There is no doubt that the expression 'everyone' is,
whether in a legal or popular sense, a wider term than the word 'person'."

[
22
]

The words used in the French language version of
the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
assist this interpretation.
"Chacun" is used where "everyone" appears in the English
version. In addition "chacun" appears in Section 19 where "any
person" is used in English. In Section 24 where the English word is
"anyone", "toute personne" is used in French. The meaning
of "personne" as found in the
Dictionnaire Juridigue Francais-Anglais

(6th edition) is "person or artificial person, body corporate deemed
fictitiously a natural person and permitted to go to law".

[
23
]

It is argued that "freedom of conscience
and religion" in
Section 2
of the
Charter
cannot apply to a corporation
because a body corporate can have neither conscience nor religion. But it has
long been held that a corporation can have the
mens rea
for a criminal
offence; it is that of its officers. If it can have a bad conscience it does
not strain language to hold that in the same manner it can have the good
conscience or even the religion of its officers. In any event, in my opinion,
this argument is irrelevant. The task of the Court is to see whether all or
part of The Lord's Day Act is inconsistent with freedom of conscience and
religion and therefore of no force or effect. It does not affect that task that
a person charged has no religion or even that he has no feelings of conscience.
It is the nature of the law which must be considered and not the attributes of
the person charged. In this context that which infringes the rights of one
Canadian, thereby infringes the rights of all. The corporation can, at the very
least, plead that it can raise the infringement of the rights of its officers,
employees and customers.

[
24
]

In
Robertson and Rosetanni v. The Queen

(supra) Cartwright, J. (as he then was) considered a similar argument which was
advanced under the Canadian Bill of Rights. Though his view was stated in a
dissenting judgment, the majority did not consider the point having reached the
conclusion that The Lord's Day Act did not offend the Canadian Bill of Rights.
At page 661, he said:

"It was argued that, in any event,
in the case at bar the appeal must fail because there is no evidence that the
appellants do not hold the religious belief that they are under no obligation
to observe Sunday. In my view such evidence would be irrelevant. The task of
the Court is to determine whether Section 4 of the Act infringes freedom of
religion. This does not depend on the religious persuasion, if any, of the
individual prosecuted but on the nature of the law. To give an extreme example,
a law providing that every person in Canada should, on pain of fine or inprisonment,
attend divine service in an Anglican Church on at least one Sunday in every
month would, in my opinion, infringe the religious freedom of every Anglican as
well as that of every other citizen."

[
25
]

It is, of course, true that there is not in the
Canadian Bill of Rights language similar to that in
Section 24
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
which gives access to the Courts to "anyone
whose rights and freedoms have been infringed or denied". But in the sense
that compulsion on one Canadian's religious freedom infringes the rights of
all, the language is equally applicable. If this were not so a legacy of the
Charter would be that a statute held to infringe the fundamental freedoms of
one individual would nevertheless continue to strike at others, leaving a
patchwork of individual liability and non-liability under the statute. In the
extreme case under The Lord's Day Act, liability would turn on whether or not
the family business had been incorporated. In my view it is the nature of the
legislation and not the attributes of the individual which must be considered.

[
26
]

Moreover, the
Charter
has both a positive and a
negative impact. Acting positively it grants and guarantees rights to
Canadians; negatively it imposes a corresponding and opposite limit on the
power of government. Everyone is guaranteed freedom of conscience and religion
but equally the same clause implicitly enjoins Parliament to make no laws which
abridge freedom of conscience and religion. The Charter imposes the negative
duty on Parliament for the benefit of all. In my view, so long as a litigant
has a status to bring the matter in question before the Court it matters not
whether he, himself, is the victim.

[
27
]

No question of standing before the Court arises
apart from the Respondent's status as a body corporate, since it was directly
charged with a criminal offence under the statute. It would therefore be within
the tests for status to make a constitutional challenge specified by the
Supreme Court of Canada in
Thorson v. Attorney General of Canada (No. 2)

(1974)
1974 CanLII 6 (SCC)
, 43 D.L.R. (3d) 1,
Nova Scotia Board of Censors v. McNeil
(1975)

1975 CanLII 14 (SCC)
, 55 D.L.R. (3d) 632 and
Minister of Justice (Canada) v. Borowski
[1982] 1
W.W.R. 977. In my opinion, therefore, this corporation may rely upon the

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
in its defence.

[
28
]

I also decline, with respect, to accede to the
argument advanced by the Attorneys General that the Provincial Court of Alberta
is not "a court of competent jurisdiction" to grant, in a suitable
case, the relief contemplated by
Section 24
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights
and Freedoms
. The first consideration is the remarkable inconvenience of such a
restricted interpretation. If the Provincial Court cannot deal with Charter
arguments, a person charged with crime and yet possessed of a valid defence under
the Charter could not raise its shield before him. Conviction and punishment
would necessarily follow until he could obtain declaratory relief in a superior
court.

[
29
]

I rely on a useful analysis of Section 24 by
Professor Gibson in
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
edited by Tarnapolski
and Beaudoin. At page 500, he points out that if express authority were
required by a court to enforce the Charter, it would remain inoperative until
appropriate federal or provincial legislation bestowed jurisdiction on the
chosen tribunals. He cites Collins, M.R. in
R. v. Garrett

(1907) 1 K.B.
881 at 886
that the phrase covers "every possible court which by enactment
is made competent to entertain a claim" and the similar, though even
broader, interpretation by Bond, C.J. in
Stringer v. Griffin

(1941) 149
S.W. (2d) 158 at 160 (Tex. App.)
. I respectfully agree with Professor Gibson's
view that

"the term 'court of competent
jurisdiction' will be construed generally: to mean any court which has,
independently of the
Charter
, jurisdiction over a situation to which the
Charter applies, or general jurisdiction to grant a remedy appropriate to
enforcement of the Charter."

[
30
]

I therefore conclude that the Provincial Court
of Alberta was a court of competent jurisdiction to rule on the defence raised
by the Respondent under the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.

[
31
]

I turn now to the two principal questions raised
by this appeal: Whether The Lord's Day Act infringes the fundamental freedom of
conscience and religion guaranteed by The
Charter of Rights
and Freedoms and,
if so, whether the statute is a reasonable limitation on that freedom.

[
32
]

Sunday observance legislation has a long history
in the western world and has existed in Canada from earliest times. A useful
historical analysis will be found in the 1970
Report on Sunday Observance
Legislation
prepared by the Ontario Law Reform Commission. The Sunday Fairs
Act of 1448 prohibited all fairs and markets on Sunday. The Sunday Observance
Act 1625, forbade meetings and assemblies of persons outside their own
parishes. The Sunday Observance Act 1627 prohibited travel on Sundays. The
Sunday Observance Act 1677, which became the principal English statute on the
subject, contained an extensive list of prohibitions and required all persons on
Sunday "to exercise themselves thereon in the duties of piety and true
religion publicly and privately". These statutes came into force in the
areas presently comprising Quebec and Ontario after 1763.

[
33
]

Subsequent legislative action in Canada on this
subject both before and after Confederation continued the religious emphasis.
As I observed earlier, the statutes on the subject between 1867 and 1903 were
all provincial enactments, a situation which ended with the Privy Council
decision declaring that the subject was within the criminal law and therefore
beyond provincial jurisdiction.

[
34
]

Canadian courts have, since that time,
consistently characterized the Sunday observance legislation as criminal law
because it deals with morality. Provincial legislators could not regulate
activities on religious holidays:
Henry Birks & Sons (Montreal) Ltd. v.
Montreal
(supra) (municipal by-law could not close shops on holy days);
Ouimet
v. Bazin
(supra) (Quebec could not ban theatrical performances on Sunday).
Parish
of St. Prosper v. Rodrigue
(1917)
1917 CanLII 598 (SCC)
, 40 D.L.R. 30 (municipal by-law could not
close restaurants on Sunday).

[
35
]

In these cases and in others appear a number of
judicial pronouncements confirming the religious basis of The Lord's Day Act,
and confirming that the purpose of the Act is one of morality - to enforce the
concept of the Christian Sunday. Because that is so, it is criminal law.
Whether it could also be criminal law if enacted for another purpose, we need
not decide. In
Robertson and Rosetanni v. The Queen

(supra) Ritchie, J.
reviewed this history and referred to The Lord's Day Act as "legislation
for the preservation of the sanctity of Sunday". The Act itself confirms
this purpose by its title, by references within it to "the Lord's
Day" and by the provision in Section 11(a) that "any necessary or
customary work in connection with divine worship " shall be deemed to be
"work of necessity or mercy". The religious purpose of The Lord's Day
Act is, in my view, beyond doubt.

[
36
]

In modern times, statutes providing for one or
more days of rest in a week could undoubtedly be so written as to be labour
legislation or health and welfare legislation. It is difficult, however, to
imagine federal legislation of this nature which would not infringe on
provincial jurisdiction though it is not necessary in this case to decide
whether such legislation could be enacted. In
Henry Birks & Sons
(Montreal) Ltd. v. Montreal
(supra) Rand, J. declined to find any purpose
other than a religious one for a by-law forbidding retail stores to open on
Roman Catholic holy days. At page 813, he said:

"That Sunday observance legislation
is within the field of the Dominion as criminal law has long been settled:
Attorney
General of Ontario v. The Hamilton Street Railway Company.
The enactments
reflecting the religious struggles of the 14-18th centuries were of public law
within the classification under our constitution of Criminal Law: they forbade
or enjoined certain conduct under pain of punishment. I cannot distinguish the
prohibition here, with sanctions for non-compliance, or carrying on business on
days given their special and common characteristic by church law from those of
that past. It is in the same category as the law of Sunday observance.

But these considerations show equally
that the statute is enacted in relation to religion; it prescribes what is in
essence a religious obligation.
We are asked to find that the purpose of the
legislation was either to give ease from labour to employees or to prevent the
sale of goods as a measure of regulating local trade and commerce
; but I
regretfully find myself unable to treat either of these contentions as having
the slightest basis or support in any pertinent consideration."

(emphasis added)

[
37
]

In the United States, a Sunday observance
statute which clearly had a religious origin was held by the Supreme Court of
the United States to have lost that character. In
McGowan v. State of
Maryland
(1961) 366 U.S. 420 the Court considered a statute which, though
it had its genesis in religion, had been substantially changed and re-enacted
to prescribe the secular goals of rest and recreation for the citizens. Terms
such as "the Lord's Day" in the statute were held to be mere
anachronisms - accidents of its history. In reaching this conclusion, the Court
noted that numerous legislative changes since the original enactment had made
"the air of the day … one of relaxation rather than religion".

[
38
]

There is probably no reason why a Canadian
statute could not be similarly re-classified. It would be necessary in
re-classifying the Lord's Day Act, however, for Parliament to demonstrate by
its amendments that it had shed its sectarian robes and further that the
re-classified law rested upon some constitutional foundation within its
competence. Again, we need not decide the feasibility of that course until it
is attempted. But without some such course of action it cannot be said that a
statute which over nearly eight decades has been found to be, in substance,
"Sunday observance" and only "Sunday observance" is now
something else. I conclude that the law has a religious purpose; it is to
enforce the Sunday of the majority of the Christian religion.

[
39
]

As a statute with a religious purpose, does The
Lord's Day Act infringe the fundamental freedom of conscience and religion? It
is said that it does so by enforcing the Christian Sunday, if not Christian
religious observance, on those whose religion requires them to observe a
different Sabbath or whose conscience forbids the observance of any Sabbath.
For those whose religion requires observance of a different Sabbath, this is
said to produce at the very least an economic dis-incentive to the practice of
their own religion and at worst a coercive atmosphere in which the nation is
perceived to require all its citizens to observe the Christian Sunday.

[
40
]

It is not desirable, in my view, at this stage
of
Charter
history to attempt a comprehensive definition of "freedom of
religion" or "freedom of conscience". The latter term seems
designed to encompass the rights of those whose fundamental principles are not
founded on theistic belief. Whatever is comprehended by the terms, however, at
the very least they mean that henceforth in Canada government shall not choose
sides in sectarian controversy. Standards shall not be imposed for purely
sectarian purposes. Sectarian observance shall neither be enforced nor
forbidden whether by economic sanction or the more subtle (but even more
devastating) means of imposing the moral power of the state on one side or the
other.

[
41
]

In the early period of Christianity, Christians
observed the same Sabbath as the Jewish religion. The change of the holy day
for most Christians from the seventh day of the week to the first day is
described by the
Report on Sunday Observance Legislation
by the Ontario
Law Reform Commission in these terms at Page 72:

"While Christianity was still within
the bosom of the Jewish faith, the commonest festival to be added to the
religious practices of Christians was the first day of the week, sometimes
referred to as the 'eighth day'. This soon came to be known as "the Lord's
day, signifying certain events recorded as having occurred on that day. First
and foremost, of course, was the resurrection of Jesus Christ reported to have
taken place on the first day of the week. Also Jesus' post-resurrection appearance
is recorded as occurring on the first day of the week. Still later, the gift of
the Holy Spirit recounted in Acts on the Feast of Pentecost is described as
taking place on the first day of the week.

……………………………………………………………………………………

The break between the Jewish observance
of the Sabbath and the Christian observance of the Lord's day was a gradual
one. It must be remembered that the strength and centre of authority for the
early Christians, who were also Jewish, was the City of Jerusalem ….……………………………………………………
However, Jerusalem was destroyed about 70 A.D., and there followed a dispersal
of Jewish Christianity. The practice of observing both the Sabbath and the
Lord's day began to fade in favour of the distinctly Christian practice of
worship on the Lord's day only."

[
42
]

Whatever the origins of the division of belief,
it is indisputable that there can now be seen among Canadians different deeply
held beliefs of religion and conscience on this subject. One group, probably
the majority, accepts Sunday as the Lord's Day. Another group consisting of
those of the Jewish faith, and Sabbatarians whose religious beliefs do not
accept Sunday as a Lord's Day distinct from Sabbath on the seventh day of the
week, believe in Saturday as their holy day. Canadians of the Muslim religion
observe Friday as their holy day. Some Canadians who have no theistic belief,
while perhaps accepting the concept of a day for rest and recreation, object to
the enforcement of a Christian Sunday.

[
43
]

Whether the economic penalty imposed by The Lord's
Day Act is an infringement of the religious freedom of those who are required
by it to refrain from business on Sunday and by their own religion on some
other day has already been considered by the Supreme Court of Canada. In
Robertson
and Rosetanni v. The Queen
(supra) the issue before the Court was whether
The Lord's Day Act infringed the right of freedom of religion "recognized
and declared" by the Canadian Bill of Rights. It will be necessary
therefore to consider whether this Court is bound in the present case by that
decision. On the financial effect of the Lord's Day Act on those whose religion
requires a holy day other than Sunday, Ritchie, J. said at pages 657-658:

"My own view is that the
effect

of the
Lord's Day Act
rather than its
purpose
must be looked to
in order to determine whether its application involves the abrogation,
abridgement or infringement of religious freedom, and I can see nothing in that
statute which in any way affects the liberty of religious thought and practice
of any citizen of this country. Nor is the 'untrammelled affirmations of
religious belief and its propagation' in any way curtailed.

The practical result of this law on those
whose religion requires them to observe a day of rest other than Sunday, is a
purely secular and financial one in that they are required to refrain from
carrying on or conducting their business on Sunday as well as on their own day
of rest. In some cases this is no doubt a business inconvenience, but it is
neither an abrogation nor an abridgement nor an infringement of religious
freedom, and the fact that it has been brought about by reason of the existence
of a statute enacted for the purpose of preserving the sanctity of Sunday,
cannot; in my view, be construed as attaching some religious significance to an
effect which is purely secular in so far as non-Christians are concerned."

[
44
]

This view may be contrasted with that expressed
by Brennan, J. in the Supreme Court of the United States in a case decided in
the same year,
Sherbert v. Verner
(1963) 374 U.S. 398. In that case the appellant held religious beliefs which
required her to observe Sabbath on Saturday. She lost her job in consequence of
her refusal to work on Saturday and was denied benefits under state
unemployment legislation on the ground that she was "not available"
to work. Brennan, J. said at page 404 in holding that the ruling infringed the
First Amendment to the Constitution:

"The ruling forces her to choose betweeen
following the precepts of her religion and forfeiting benefits, on the one
hand, and abandoning one of the precepts of her religion in order to accept
work, on the other hand. Governmental imposition of such a choice puts the same
kind of burden upon the free exercise of religion as would a fine imposed
against appellant for her Saturday worship."

[
45
]

In many cases, the term "business
inconvenience" will not be an apt term to describe the financial or
"secular" effect of being permitted only five days of business
activity in a week rather than six. In the face of greater activity permitted a
competitor, the "inconvenience" may become financial ruin. Whatever
its degree, The Lord's Day Act, in my opinion, imposes a coercive burden on the
free exercise of religion or conscience. Like Brennan, J., I can see little difference
between the practical effect of that burden and a penalty imposed for Saturday
(or Friday) worship.

[
46
]

Moreover, emphasis on economic effects alone
ignores an even more serious burden: the coercive effect of the statute in
imposing the Christian Sunday on all persons, Christians and non-Christians,
alike. Good citizens obey the law; for many Canadians able to bear or ignore
any economic penalty of obedience, the imposition of the Christian Sunday using
the force of the state to do it far outweighs any economic consideration.

[
47
]

It is urged that there is no breach of the

Charter
because the practical effect of The Lord's Day Act is minimal, perhaps
because of uneven enforcement. That argument, however, denies a breach of the
Charter by invoking
Section 1
a course to be followed only after it is
determined that there has been a breach. Moreover the effect of The Lord's Day
Act is hardly minimal. Apart altogether from economic dis-incentives, the moral
power of the state has been imposed on one side of a dispute between its
citizens in which the state must take no part. Thereby, there has occurred a
serious infringement of the fundamental freedom of conscience and religion.

[
48
]

I respectfully agree with the dissenting
judgment of Cartwright, J. in
Robertson and Rosetanni v. The Queen

(supra) when he said at pages 660-61:

"I can find no answer to the
argument of counsel for the appellant, that the purpose and the effect of the
Lord's
Day Act
are to compel, under the penal sanctions of the Criminal law, the
observance of Sunday as a religious holy day by all the inhabitants of Canada;
that this is an infringement of religious freedom I do not doubt.

I agree with my brother Ritchie that the
following words which he quotes from the judgment of

Frankfurter J. in
Board of Education
v. Barnette, supra
, are appropriate to describe the freedom of religion
referred to in the
Canadian Bill of Rights
:

Its essence
is freedom from conformity to religious dogma, not freedom from conformity to
law

because of religious dogma.

But this passage presupposes that the
word 'law' which I have italicized means a law which has a constitutionally
valid purpose and effect other than the forbidding or commanding of conduct in
a solely religious aspect.

In my opinion a law which compels a
course of conduct, whether positive or negative, for a purely religious purpose
infringes the freedom of religion.

A law which, on solely religious grounds,
forbids the pursuit on Sunday of an otherwise lawful activity differs in
degree, perhaps, but not in kind from a law which commands a purely religious
course of conduct on that day, such as for example, the attendance at least
once at divine service in a specified church."

[
49
]

Unless, therefore, I am precluded from so doing
by the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada in
Robertson and Rosetanni v.
The Queen
, I would hold that The Lord's Day Act infringes upon the freedom
of religion and conscience guaranteed by the
Charter of Rights
and Freedoms. I
must therefore consider whether that case, decided under the Canadian Bill of Rights,
requires this Court to reach the same conclusion under the Charter.

[
50
]

The first difference at once apparent between
the Bill and the
Charter
is that the Bill is declaratory. By Section 1 of the
Bill it is:

"recognized and declared that in
Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by
reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the following human
rights and fundamental freedoms, namely,

(c)    freedom of religion."

[
51
]

This declaratory language is the foundation of
the Court's conclusion in
Robertson and Rosetanni
.
At page 654 Ritchie,
J. said:

"It is to be noted at the outset
that the Canadian Bill of Rights is not concerned with 'human rights and
fundamental freedoms' in any abstract sense, but rather with such "rights
and freedoms' as they existed in Canada immediately before the statute was
enacted (See also s. 5(1)). It is therefore 'the religious freedom'
then
existing in this country that is safe-guarded
by the provisions of
s. 2

which read, in part as follows:

Every law of
Canada shall, unless it is expressly declared by an Act of the Parliament of
Canada that it shall operate notwithstanding the Canadian Bill of Rights, be so
construed and applied as not to abrogate, abridge or infringe or to authorize
the abrogation, abridgement or infringement of any of the rights or freedoms
herein recognized and declared

…

It is accordingly of first importance to
understand the concept of religious freedom which was recognized in this
country before the enactment of the Canadian Bill of Rights and after the
enactment of the Lord's Day Act in its present form."

(emphasis added)

[
52
]

Thus the declaratory language of Section 1 of
The Canadian Bill of Rights had a double effect; the right itself is defined by
the state of the law in 1960 and the protection afforded is limited by the same
definition. In
The Queen v. Drybones

1969 CanLII 1 (SCC)
, [1970] S.C.R. 282, the Court did,
nevertheless, hold a section of the Indian Act inoperative because it could not
be "sensibly construed" so as not to abrogate, abridge or infringe
one of the rights and freedoms declared by The Bill of Rights to exist.
Ritchie, J. then commented on his own decision in
Robertson and Rosetanni

at pages 295 and 296 and said that the case did not mean that "freedom of
religion" as declared in The Bill of Rights was circumscribed by the
provisions of the Canadian statutes in force at the date of its enactment.
However, in
Attorney General Canada v. Lavell

1973 CanLII 175 (SCC)
, [1974] S.C.R. 1349 at
1365, Ritchie, J. said:

"In my view the meaning to be given
to the language employed in the
Bill of Rights
is the meaning which it
bore in Canada at the time when the Bill was enacted, and it follows that the
phrase 'equality before the law' is to be construed in light of the law
existing in Canada at that time."

[
53
]

Similarly in
R. v. Burnshine
(1974)
1974 CanLII 150 (SCC)
, 25
C.R.N.S. 270 at 277, Martland, J. said:

"I am not prepared to accept the
respondent's submissions as to the meaning of the phrase 'equality before the
law' in s. 1(b) of the Bill of Rights. Section 1 of the Bill declared that six
defined human rights and freedoms 'have existed' and that they should 'continue
to exist'. All of them had existed and were protected under the common law. The
Bill did not purport to define new rights and freedoms. What it did was to declare
their existence in a statute, and further by
s. 2
, to protect them from
infringement by any federal statute."

[
54
]

The Charter avoided the declaratory language
which produced this interpretation of The Canadian Bill of Rights. Section 1
"guarantees the rights and freedoms set out"; Section 2 states that
"everyone has the … fundamental freedoms". This language does not
require that the defination of either the right or protection of the right be
limited by the law in existence when it was enacted. The
Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms
will grow with Canada; it will survive and flourish with
changing perceptions and a changing society.

[
55
]

The most fundamental difference between the

Charter
and the Bill is the enhanced status of the Charter as part of "the
supreme law of Canada". (Section 52(1)). It is not merely a declaration of
existing law or a tool for use in statutory construction. By Section 24 the
Judiciary is charged with the task of devising appropriate remedies for
infringement. This enhanced status of the Charter as well as the different
language in it, require the conclusion, in my opinion, that
Robertson and Rosetanni

does not apply to Charter cases. It does not preclude a finding by this Court
that The Lord's Day Act infringes the fundamental freedom of religion and
conscience given by the Charter.

[
56
]

The final question to be decided is whether this
statute is within the limitation of
Section 1
of the
Charter
and so is a
reasonable limit to the freedom "demonstrably justified in a free and
democratic society". As did Associate Chief Justice McKinnon in
Re Southam
Inc. and the Queen
(supra), I feel myself to be "wandering in
unexplored territory" in interpreting the meaning and effect of the words
in Section 1 of the Charter though the path through the wilderness is easier to
find now that he has been there.

[
57
]

There is a tension at once apparent between
section 1 and the remainder of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. The
Charter eloquently states individual rights and limitations on government to protect
them. Section 1 then says that nevertheless there are circumstances where
infringement of those rights is reasonable. It requires, perhaps for the first
time in our national history, that Judges articulate the fundamental values of
society and set their order of priority. In each case where Section 1 is
invoked we will be called upon to decide whether a given societal value is more
important than one or the other of the fundamental rights and freedoms
guaranteed by the Charter.

[
58
]

I respectfully agree with Associate Chief
Justice McKinnon in
Re Southam Inc. and the Queen
(
supra
) and
with Chief Justice Deschênes in
Quebec Protestant Association of Protestant
School Boards v. Le Procureur General du Quebec (No. 2)

1982 CanLII 3268 (QC CS)
, 140 D.L.R. (3d) 33 at 59 that the burden of proving an exception under

Section 1
of the
Charter
rests on the party claiming the benefit of the
limitation. In this case that is the appellant.

[
59
]

Associate Chief Justice McKinnon established the
guide post for his journey into the unknown as follows at page 29:

"In determining the reasonableness
of the limit in each particular case, the court must examine objectively its
argued rational basis in light of what the court understands to be reasonable
in a free and democratic society. Further, there is, it appears to me, a
significant burden on the proponent of the limit or limits to demonstrate their
justification to the satisfaction of the court. As I said earlier that may be
easily done in a number of cases."

[
60
]

What societal value is offered in this case to
legitimize breach of the fundamental freedom of conscience and religion? It is
that there are reasons other than religious reasons for enacting statutes
similar to this one. It is said that a day of rest on some day of the week is
such a universally recognized requirement of society that it is reflected in
legislation throughout the western world. The day chosen is usually Sunday
merely because that has become the habit of society. It is urged that because
that habit originated in statutes with a religious genesis makes no real
difference to the basic interest being promoted.

[
61
]

The difficulty with this argument in my view is
the undoubted religious aspect of The Lord's Day Act. As criminal law it is
federal legislation because it is religious legislation. That is its
fundamental purpose and effect; it is almost accidental that it also achieves
aims of rest and recreation for our citizens. It enforces not merely a day of
rest, but the Christian Sunday. If a statute in some other form would be
unobjectionable the obvious answer is for the legislative body with the
competence to do so to enact it.

[
62
]

Moreover, the Lord's Day Act offers little in
the way of compromise. There are few exemptions from its prohibitions. A
statute enacted for health reasons or as labour legislation might be expected
to have exemptions for those whose religion required their absence from gainful
activity on some day other than that chosen, and who actually observe that day
of rest. We were referred to statutes with such provisions in Connecticut
(Conn. Gen. Stat. 1958 rev., ss. 55-303), Kentucky (Ken. Rev. Stat. 1959, ss.
436-160), Maine (Me. R.S. 1954, C. 134, ss. 44), Michigan (Mich. Stat. Ann.
1957 rev. ss. 18.855), Oklahoma (Okla. Stat. Ann. 1958 tit. 21 ss. 909) and
Vermont (Vt. Stat. Ann. 1959 Rev.).

[
63
]

Whether Parliament could enforce as a matter of
religion and morality a Sabbath day with the day of the week to be chosen by
each citizen would present more problems under the
Charter
. In any event the
validity of such an approach need not be considered until it is attempted.
Whether or not an existing statute can be "read down" in order to
comply with the Charter, I am of the opinion that we cannot, in fulfilling our
task under Section 1 or
Section 24
, write new sections or rules so that the
statute becomes a more reasonable limit on the Charter freedoms. That view was
also expressed by Martin, J. in
R. v. Oakes
(1983)
1983 CanLII 1850 (ON CA)
, 40 O.R. (2d) 660 at
683 and by McKinnon, A.C.J. in
R. v. Southam
(supra) at page 38.

[
64
]

For these reasons I would dismiss the appeal.

[

Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms

and
articles 1
and
2
thereof provide as follows:

"Whereas Canada is founded upon
principles that recognize the supremacy of God and the rule of Law:

Guarantee of Rights and Freedoms

Canadian Charter of Rights
and Freedoms

to such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in
a free and democratic society.

fundamental freedoms:

(a) freedom
of conscience and religion;

(b) .…

(c)  .…

(d) .…"

[
73
]

As I will also be referring to the French
version of these provisions, I include it now:

Attendu que le Canada est fondé sur des principes
qui reconnaissent la suprématie de Dieu et la primauté du droit:

1.     La
Charte canadienne des droits
et libert)s
garantit les droits et libertés qui y sont énoncés. … .

suivantes:

a)   liberté
de conscience et de religion;

b)   .…

c)   .…
