."

[
74
]

In considering the meaning of "freedom of
conscience and religion", it is helpful to review briefly the historical
development of the principle of religious liberty. It was born in reaction to
repression by ruling authority of religious beliefs and practices not
conforming to its own and to attempts by the rulers to impose their own
religious beliefs and practices upon their subjects. In the nations of
antiquity, attention focused on public display rather than on belief, and
participation in the public worship of the national gods was required
irrespective of belief. In the development of western civilization, we see that
after the Roman emperors adopted Christianity, religious doctrine became a
subject matter for political attention. This increased when the mantle of
political power passed to the Church with the fall of the Roman Empire. Courts
of inquisition were set up to stamp out doctrinal deviation. Heresy was sought
out and punished. This excessive proselytism did not stop with the advent of
the Reformation. Nations with established reformed churches continued to punish
dissension from the dogma of the established church. Religious non-conformity was
equated with political non-conformity and treated as a seditious threat to
power. England experienced religious persecutions, by one faction after the
other, so harsh and intolerant that its people were driven to emigration in
large numbers. Many of those who came to the New World brought with them the
same intolerance which they had sought to escape and themselves legislated
repression of others, usually in the form of civil disabilities. It was in
consequence of this repression, both in the mother land and in the new
colonies, that the concept of religious liberty gained its first foothold in
the American colonies. It was first included in the Charter of Rhode Island in
1663. The concept spread to other colonies and nations and was subsequently
written into several States' constitutions. In the first draft of the
Constitution of the United States, the only reference to religious freedom was
the provision in Article VI prohibiting religious tests as a requirement for
holding public office.

[
75
]

In 1789. the National Assembly of France adopted
its "Declaration des droits de l'homme et du citoyen" which included
freedom of religion in Article X in the following terms:

"Nul ne doit être
inguiété

pour ses opinions, même religieuses, pourvu que leur manifestation ne trouble
pas l'ordre public etabli par la loi"

[
76
]

The entire declaration was made the preamble to
the constitution of 1791.

[
77
]

The first amendment to the Constitution of the
United States also passed in 1791 adopted the present wording with respect to
freedom of religion:

AMENDMENT I

Congress shall make no law respecting an
establishment of religion, or
prohibiting the free exercise thereof
: or
abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people
peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of
grievances.

[
78
]

The right to religious freedom was subsequently
written into the constitutions of many nations down to and including the
Canadian
Charter
.
It is recognized as one of the fundamental human rights to which
every human person is entitled by reason of being endowed with free will and
intelligence. It derives from natural law and not from positive law. It is the
same for all humans, of all nations and of all eras. In
The Oxford Companion
to Law,
David M. Walker, Regius Professor of Law in the University of
Glasgow, the learned author at page 591 defines human rights as:

"Claims asserted as those which
should be, or sometimes stated to be those which are, legally recognized and
protected to secure for each individual the fullest and freest development of
personality and spiritual, moral and other independence.
They are conceived
of as rights inherent in individuals as rational, free-willing creatures, not
conferred by mere positive law, nor capable of being abridged or abrogated by
positive law.

The origins of assertions of human rights
are to be found in the ideas of natural law and natural rights. These ideas
were developed by the Greek and Roman Stoics, by the Roman lawyers and the
Christian fathers, and by Aquinas and some of the mediaeval English jurists, as
the basis of the beliefs in the freedom and equality of all men: the crucial
case was slavery, which positive law commonly recognized but natural law
condemned.

.… From the seventeenth century, the law
of nature was utilized as a basis of modern international law. … . The founders
of modern international law stressed the value and importance of the natural
rights of man. Vitoria asserted that the primitive peoples of America were
entitled to the protection of law and justice."

[
79
]

The universal human rights movement gained
urgent momentum in consequence of the atrocities of World War II.

[
80
]

Thus it was declared one of the world aims of
American policy by President F.D. Roosevelt in an address to Congress on
January 6, 1941.

"In the future days, which we seek
to make secure, we look forward to a world founded upon four essential human
freedoms:

The first is freedom of speech and
expression - everywhere in the world.

The second is freedom of every person to
worship God in his own way, everywhere in the world.

The third (etc.)"

[
81
]

In the

Universal Declaration of Human
Rights

adopted by the General Assembly of
the United Nations on December 10, 1948, it is provided as follows in Article
18:

"Art. 18. Everyone has the right to
freedom of thought, conscience and religion; this right includes freedom to
change his religion or belief, and freedom, either alone or in community with
others and in public or private, to manifest his religion or belief in
teaching, practice, worship and observance."

[
82
]

Next, and to the same effect is Article 9 of the

European Convention for the Protectin of Human Rights and Fundamantal
Freedoms
signed on November 4, 1950. and coining into force on September 3,
1953.

"(1)  Everyone has the right to
freedom of thought, conscience and religion; this right includes freedom to
change his religion or belief and freedom, either alone or in community with
others and in public or private, to manifest his religion or belief, in
worship, teaching practice and observance.

(2)    Freedom to manifest one's religion
or beliefs shall be subject only to such limitations as are prescribed by law
and are necessary in a democratic society in the interests of public safety,
for the protection of public order, health or morals, or for the protection of
the rights and freedoms of others."

[
83
]

Then comes the
Canadian Bill of Rights
passed
by the Parliament of Canada and assented to August 10, 1960:

1.     It is hereby recognized and
declared that in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without
discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the
following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely,

(a)    .…

(b)    .…

(c)    freedom
of religion

(d)    .…

(e)    .…

(f)     .…

[
84
]

This Bill could affect only the federal field
but most Canadian Provinces moved to supplement it by enacting
Bills of
Rights
of their own.

[
85
]

Of particular significance is the
International
Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
adopted by the General Assembly of
the United Nations on December 16, 1966 and open for signature on December 19,
1966. Article 18 of that document is as follows:

"1.          Everyone shall have the
right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion. This right shall include
freedom to have or to adopt a religion or belief of his choice, and freedom,
either individually or in community with others and in public or private, to
manifest his religion or belief in worship, observance, practice and teaching.

2.           No one shall be subject to
coercion which would impair his freedom to have or to adopt a religion or
belief of his choice.

3.           Freedom to manifest one's
religion or beliefs may be subject only to such limitations as are prescribed
by law and are necessary to protect public safety, order, health, or morals or
the fundamental rights and freedoms of others.

4.           The States Parties to the
present Covenant undertake to have respect for the liberty of parents and, when
applicable, legal guardians to ensure the religious and moral education of
their children in conformity with their own convictions."

[
86
]

Canada adhered to that covenant in 1976.

[
87
]

A proviso to the same effect is found in the
American
Convention for Human Rights
adopted by members of the Organization of
American States.

[
88
]

Thus it can be seen that the
Canadian Charter

was not conceived and born in isolation. It is part of the universal human
rights movement. It guarantees that the power of government in Canada shall not
be used to abridge or abrogate the fundamental rights to which every Canadian,
as well as every other human being in the world, is entitled by birth. The
Charter

can be divided into two parts, one dealing with fundamental human rights in
harmony with the
International Covenant
, the other dealing with matters
peculiar to Canada. It is of course in the first part
that
s.2
of the Charter must fall.

[
89
]

That these fundamental freedoms were entrenched
in the
Charter

in conformity with Canada's commitment in the
International
Convenant
cannot be doubted. Even the
Canadian Bill of Rights
adopted
before the
International Covenant,
was intended to link Canada with the
worldwide movement for human rights. This was underlined by the Prime Minister,
John G. Diefenbaker, when speaking to the Bill. He said:

"This measure that I introduce is
the first step on the part of Canada to carry out the acceptance either of the
international declaration of human rights or of the principles that actuated
those who produced that noble document."

[
90
]

It is in this historical universal context that
the expression "freedom of conscience and religion" used in the
Canadian
Charter

should be defined. Freedom of religion in the
Charter
has
the same meaning as freedom of religion in the
International Covenant
and
in the other documents on human rights to which I have referred, including the
Canadian
Bill of Rights.
The concept is aimed at the elimination of oppression and
repression by civil authority on account of religious belief, or compulsion to
accept any particular doctrine. It has nothing at all to do with equal
treatment of all religious sects within any given nation. This is the meaning
ascribed to the expression "liberty of conscience" in the
dictionaries of both official languages.

[
91
]

The word "freedom" is synonymous with
the word "liberty" and indeed the French version of the
Charter

uses
the word "liberte" in clauses 1 and 2.

[
92
]

In Oxford's Unabridged Dictionary the expression
is defined as follows:

"Liberty
of conscience: the system of things in which a member of a state is permitted
to follow
without interference
the dictates of his conscience in the
profession of any religious creed or the exercise of any mode of worship."

[
93
]

Random House Dictionary of the English language
in its coverage of synonyms at the end of the definition of freedom says that

"freedom, independence, liberty
refer to an
absence of undue restrictions
and an opportunity to exercise
one's rights and powers".

[
94
]

Bélisle in Dictionnaire Nord-Americain de la
Langue Francaise defines
libert) de conscience
as follows:

"Liberté
de conscience, droit d'adopter les opinions religieuses que l'on croit vraies,
sans
tomber sous le coup d'aucune loi pénale.
"

[
95
]

For the present purposes the word
"religion" added in
Article 2(a)
of the
Charter
can be treated as
synonymous with "conscience". Freedom of conscience includes the
right not to have any religion at all: freedom of religion includes not only
the right to hold religious beliefs, but also to practice the religion of one's
choice, subject of course to the restriction in
Article 1
.

[
96
]

In the case of
Walter v. A.G. Alberta,
(1969)

1969 CanLII 64 (SCC)
, S.C.R. 383, Martland, J. defined religion as follows:

"Religion, as the subject matter of
legislation, wherever the jurisdiction may lie, must mean religion in the sense
that it is generally understood in Canada. It involves matters of faith and
worship, and freedom of religion involves freedom in connection with the
profession and dissemination of religious faith and the exercise of religious
worship."

[
97
]

In considering whether the
Lord's Day Act
infringes
on the freedom of conscience and religion guaranteed by the
Charter of
Rights

the court must determine whether that Act interferes with the
exercise of that freedom as above defined.

[
98
]

In my view, the effect of the
Lord's Day Act
upon
religious freedom has already been effectively and authoritatively settled by
the Supreme Court of Canada in
Robertson and Rosetanni v. The Queen

1963 CanLII 17 (SCC)
, 1963,
S.C.R. 651. In that case, as in the case before us, the appeal was from a
conviction for a violation of s.4 of the
Lord's Day Act.
It was
contended by the appellants that the
Lord's Day Act
was in conflict with
the
Canadian Bill of Rights
and its declaration of the right of freedom
of religion.

[
99
]

In rejecting the appeal Ritchie, J. delivering
the majority judgment said at p.657:

"My own view is that the
effect

of the
Lord's Day Act
rather than its
purpose
must be looked to
in order to determine whether its application involves the abrogation,
abridgement or infringement of religious freedom, and I can see nothing in that
statute which in any way affects the liberty of religious thought and practice
of any citizen of this country. Nor is the 'untrammelled affirmations of
religious belief and its propagation' in any way curtailed.

The practical result of this law on those
whose religion requires them to observe a day of rest other than Sunday, is a
purely secular and financial one in that they are required to refrain from
carrying on or conducting their business on Sunday as well as on their own day
of rest. In some cases this is no doubt a business inconvenience, but it is
neither an abrogation nor an abridgement nor an infringement of religious
freedom, and the fact that it has been brought about by reason of the existence
of a statute enacted for the purpose of preserving the sanctity of Sunday,
cannot, in my view, be construed as attaching some religious significance to an
effect which is purely secular in so far as non-Christians are concerned."

[
100
]

It is argued by the respondent and intervenors
in its support before us that the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in
Robertson
and Rosetanni

is not binding upon us because the
Canadian Bill of Rights

only defined religious freedom as it existed in Canada at the time of the
enactment of the
Canadian Bill of Rights,
whereas the rights guaranteed
by the
Charter of Rights

granted and protected religious freedom without
reference to the freedoms then existing in Canada so that the religious freedom
which we are now considering under the
Charter of Rights
is something
quite different from the religious freedom referred to in the
Canadian Bill
of Rights.
Having thus freed us from the binding authority of
Robertson
and Rosetanni
the respondent and intervenors would then invite us to adopt
the minority view of Cartwright, J. in
Robertson and Rosetanni
.
He said
in his dissenting reasons at p.660:

"I can find no answer to the
argument of counsel for the appellant, that the purpose and the effect of the
Lord's
Day Act
are to compel, under the penal sanctions of the Criminal law, the
observance of Sunday as a religious holy day by all the inhabitants of Canada;
that this is an infingement of religious freedom I do not doubt.

I agree with my brother Ritchie that the
following words which he quotes from the judgment of Frankfurter J. in
Board
of Education v. Barnette, supra,
are appropriate to describe the freedom of
religion referred to in the
Canadian Bill of Rights:

Its essence
is freedom from conformity to religious dogma, not freedom from conformity to
law

because of religious dogma.

But this passage presupposes that the
word 'law' which I have italicized means a law which has a constitutionally
valid purpose and effect other than the forbidding or commanding of conduct in
a solely religious aspect.

In my opinion a law which compels a
course of conduct, whether positive or negative, for a purely religious purpose
infringes the freedom of religion.

A law which, on solely religious grounds,
forbids the pursuit on Sunday of an otherwise lawful activity differs in
degree, perhaps, but not in kind from a law which commands a purely religious
course of conduct on that day, such as for example, the attendance at least
once at divine service in a specified church."

[
101
]

In my view the distinction made by the
respondent and intervenors in the nature of the right to freedom of religion
secured by the Canadian
Bill of Rights
and that guaranteed by the
Charter

is not a valid distinction. The
Charter
does not purport to change the
meaning of words and in particular the meaning of "freedom of conscience
and religion" as traditionally and universally understood and earlier
defined as the birthright of every human being. The "freedom of
religion" declared and secured by the
Canadian Bill of Rights
in
1960 and considered by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Robertson and Rosetanni

has the same meaning as the "freedom of conscience and religion"
guaranteed by the
Charter of Rights
in 1981. The effect of the
Lord's
Day Act
upon that same freedom of conscience and religion has been decided
in
Robertson and Rosetanni
.
While it may be technically true that this
court is not bound in this case by
Robertson and Rosetanni

because the
two cases deal with different documents, yet the interpretation by the Supreme
Court of Canada of the same provision of the
Lord's Day Act
and the same
fundamental right of freedom of conscience and religion is compelling.

[
102
]

Furthermore in my view and with all due respect
to Cartwright, J., it is inaccurate to say that the
Lord's Day Act
compels
the observance of Sunday
as a religious holy day
by all the inhabitants
of Canada. The
Lord's Day Act
does no such thing; it compels neither
Christian nor non-Christian to observe Sunday
as a religious holy day.
A
distinction must be made between mere observance of Sunday as a day of rest by
observing the prohibitions in the Act and the observance of Sunday as a
religious
holy day.
While the legislation was undoubtedly religiously motivated to
conform to the desires of the large Christian majority of the day its purpose
was not compulsion or interference with the religions of others. The sponsors
of the Act made that clear. In speaking to the Bill Prime Minister Laurier said
this:

"I say, … that the very basis of any
legislation of this kind must be to give the civil sanction, the sanction of
the positive law to the moral law and the divine law. That is the basis which I
lay down and upon which this measure proceeds. But this measure, while it lays
down this principle, does not go into the application of that principle. The
law does not provide that a man on Sunday shall be obliged to go to church,
shall be obliged to wear certain garments, to do certain things upon this line
and that; the liberty of the subject is not interfered with in that respect,
and a man can do on the Sabbath whatever he pleases to do."

[
103
]

Nor does the
Lord's Day Act
have the
effect

of compelling observance of Sunday
as a religious holy day.
The
compulsion to attend church services found in predecessor English statutes has
been removed. The sale of goods or the performance of labour are, per se, void
of religious significance, and so is the abstention from these activities. It
is only to the extent that these secular acts are shrouded with personal
religious cult or belief that they acquire a religious color. All worship is
accompanied by ordinary human acts, be it silent meditation, raising of arms,
kneeling or prostration. These physical acts are capable of becoming religious
symbols and receiving religious significance only by the free choice of the
actor. The floor layer who kneels to lay his tile is not thereby performing a
religious act. The person sunning on the beach or resting in the park is not
observing Sunday
as a religious holy day.
The observance of the Lord's
Day as a
religious holy day
is a matter of personal choice in keeping
with the freedom of conscience guaranteed by
Article 2(a)
of the
Charter
.

[
104
]

We are also urged by the appellant and the intervenors
to apply a liberal interpretation to
Article 2(a)
of the
Charter

to
include a prohibition against established religion in the nature of that found
in the first amendment to the Constitution of the United States. This would
prohibit legislation having the appearance of preferment of one religion over
another, or of legislative accommodation to one sect without the same
accommodation to others.

[
105
]

The principles of construction to be applied to
the
Charter
were considered in relation to
Article 8
of the Charter by Prowse,
J. of this court in
Southam Inc. v. Lawson A.W. Hunter et al
(1983),
1983 ABCA 32 (CanLII)
, 3
C.C.C. (3d) 497, where he quoted and adopted the following rule of construction
used by the Privy Council in interpreting the Bermuda Constitution in
Minister
of Home Affairs v. Fisher
(1980) A.C. 319
and expressed as follows by Lord
Wilberforce:

'In their Lordships' view there are two
possible answers to this. The first would be to say that, recognising the
status of the Constitution as, in effect, an Act of Parliament, there is room
for interpreting it with less rigidity, and greater generosity, than other
Acts, such as those which are concerned with property, or succession, or
citizenship. … The second would be more radical: it would be to treat a
constitutional instrument such as this as sui generis, calling for principles
of interpretation of its own, suitable to its character as already described,
without necessary acceptance of all the presumptions that are relevant to
legislation of private law.

… Their Lordships prefer the second. This
is in no way to say that there are no rules of law which should apply to the
interpretation of a Constitution. A Constitution is a legal instrument giving
rise, amongst other things, to individual rights capable of enforcement in a court
of law.
Respect must be paid to the language which has been used and to the
traditions and usages which have given meaning to that language.
It is
quite consistent with this, and with the recognition that rules of
interpretation may apply, to take as a point of departure for the process of
interpretation
a recognition of the character and origin of the instrument
,
and to be guided by the principle of giving full recognition and effect to
those fundamental rights and freedoms with a statement of which the
Constitution commences."

[
106
]

As previously shown, the character and origin of
the
Charter
,
insofar as it deals with fundamental freedoms, clearly
derives from the universal movement. The meaning and usage of words in that
movement should be the basis for construction of the same words in the
Charter.

[
107
]

The anti-establishment provision in the
Constitution of the United States is peculiar to that country and has been
adopted only by Australia. It is the product of positive law, not of natural
law, and has accordingly nothing to do with the fundamental freedom of
religion. It was added to the constitution in the wake of the French Revolution
which had swept away autocrtatic rule by an alliance of royalty and church. It
is noteworthy that 10 of the 13 American colonies then had some form of church
establishment. This political situation which was aimed by anti-establishment
has since evaporated. Reference to anti-establishment is noticeably absent from
the
American Convention for Human Rights.
Separation of church and state
in this country as in England has effectively been achieved through evolution
of law. This separation has been recognized by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Chaput
v. Roma
in
1955 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, 1955 S.C.R. 834 and in
Saumur v. The City of Quebec
(1953)

1953 CanLII 3 (SCC)
, 2 S.C.R. 299. There was accordingly no need to entrench in the
Charter

what
was already confirmed by the Supreme Court. United States judicial decisions on
anti-establishment are accordingly of little assistance in interpreting the
Charter.

[
108
]

In an article entitled "Freedom of
Assembly, Association, Conscience, and Religion" by Irwin Cotler found in
the text edited by Tarnopolsky and Beaudoin,
Canadian Chatter of Rights and
Freedoms,
(1982) the author states the following concerning the freedom of
religion in Canada, at p.201:

However, as we have seen, freedom of
religion in the United States, and in Australia for that matter, includes not
only a guarantee against the abridgement of the free exercise of religion, but
a guarantee against the establishment of religion. In Canada, on the other
hand, separation of church and state has never been an avowed policy of
Canadian legislators, and indeed, the incorporation of s.93 into the
Charter
,
together with the reference in the Preamble to the Supreme Deity, would seem to
evince a contrary legislative intention, let alone a distinguishable legal
culture. Also, what are we to make of the Proclamation of the Constitution Act,
1982 which begins with the words 'In the year of our Lord'?

Moreover, the very fact that the Supreme
Court upheld the Lord's Day Act, which was enacted to safeguard the sanctity of
Sunday in support of Christian religious tenets, could lead to the contrary
conclusion that freedom of religion in Canada is intended to include only a
guarantee against infringement of its free exercise, and not a guarantee
against the establishment of religion."

[
109
]

I agree with that view. It can be assumed that
the drafters and sponsors of the
Canadian Charter

were familiar with the
anti-establishment provisions of the Constitution of the United States in that
respect, and familiar also with some of the results flowing from the broad
interpretation of it by the courts in that country which would be deemed
undesirable in this country. The omission of that provision from the
Canadian
Chatter
was obviously intentional. It goes beyond the requirement in the
International

Covenant. Canadian courts ought not to import it into the
Charter.

[
110
]

That anti-establishment was not intended in the
Charter

is manifest by
s.29
which provides:

"Nothing in this
Charter
abrogates
or derogates from any rights or privileges guaranteed by or under the
Constitution of Canada in respect of denominational, separate or dissentient
schools.

[
111
]

That is clearly incompatible with the
anti-establishment doctrine. If freedom of religion has an anti-establishment
connotation in the
International Convenant.
Section 29 violates rather
than conforms to the
International Covenant
.

[
112
]

It is realistic to recognize that the Canadian
nation is a part of "Western" or European civilization molded in and
impressed with Christian values and traditions. These remain a strong
constituent element in the basic fabric of our society. English law in
particular bears the imprint of canon law, some of which is in turn a
modification of Roman law. The extent of the influence of Christianity on our
legal and social systems is outlined in The Oxford Campanion to Law:

"Not least, it is necessary to
consider the influence of Christianity and the Bible on Western legal systems.
These factors have influenced law in at least five distinct ways; firstly, by
influencing the law of nature theory; secondly, by directly supplying rules
which were enacted or followed; thus the Scots statutes regulating the degree
of relationship for marriage and incest expressly incorporate the relevant
verses of Leviticus 18; thirdly, by reinforcing ethical principles and
providing an underlying justification for rules of statute or common law, e.g.
the punishment of murder, theft, and adultery; fourthly, by influencing law in
a humanitarian direction, emphasizing the worth of the individual, the
protection of dependants and children, and the sanctity of life; and fifthly,
justifying and emphasizing the maintenance of moral standards, notions of
honesty, good faith, fairness, and others. The commonest single aspect of
Christian influence on law is the oath, which many persons must take on various
occasions, the sovereign to uphold Church and State, the judge to administer
law justly, and most commonly, the witness to tell the truth. In the last case
the underlying belief in the oath is that the force of religious belief will
compel the witness to tell the truth, and that, if he does not. God will punish
him."

[
113
]

I do not believe that the political sponsors of
the
Charter

intended to confer upon the courts the task of stripping
away all vestiges of those values and traditions, and the courts should be most
loathe to assume that role. With the
Lord's Day Act
eliminated, will not
all reference in the statutes to Christmas. Easter, or Thanksgiving be next?
What of the use of the Gregorian Calendar. Such interpretation would make of
the
Charter
an instrument for the repression of the majority at the
instance of every dissident and result in an amorphous, rootless and Godless
nation contrary to the recognition of the Supremacy of God declared in the
preamble. The "living tree" will wither if planted in sterilized
soil.

[
114
]

Neither the
Canadian Charter
nor the
European
Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms
nor
the
United Nations Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
proscribe
legislation designed or having the effect of favoring the religion of the
majority or of accommodating any particular religious group in any specific
instance. The desirability of doing so is a matter of internal political
expedience. It is not inconsistent with the basic principles of democracy or
the
Charter
that the views of the majority should receive preferred
attention from government, provided that the rights of others are not thereby
diminished.

[
115
]

England, the source of our law maintains a state
religion; all other religions are merely tolerated. It fully recognizes freedom
of conscience and religion, although in English law the power to regulate, or
control, or ban it still rests with the supreme Parliament, as it did in Canada
before the
Charter
.
The Presbyterian Church is the established church of
Scotland, although independent of state control. Yet the United Kingdom has
committed itself to the
European Convention.
Several other nations who
are members of the United Nations have state religions while recognizing
freedom of religion.

[
116
]

A law having a religious purpose or effect will
violate the
Charter

only if its objective or effect is to oppress or
interfere with religious liberty. The objectives of government and churches
frequently overlap, particularly in the social and moral spheres. A church
sponsored social programme may very well coincide with a valid objective of
government and guite properly receive government financial assistance in this country.
As much as it may be desirable and fair that all religious preferences be
treated equally, there are times when that is not possible. The
Lord's Day
Act
is an example. Civil authority, while bowing to pressure from religious
groups, recognized the moral value of a day of rest. That it should have
selected the day of the week regarded as holy by the great majority of
Canadians is not inconsistent with the basic principles of democracy. That is
political reality. Majority rule is restricted by the
Charter
only when
it abridges or abrogates the guaranteed rights of others. An Islamic nation may
prohibit the consumption of alcohol on religious grounds; that does not coerce
its non-islamic inhabitants to accept the Koran. India may pass legislation
prohibiting the killing of cows out of respect for the religious beliefs of
some of its people; that does not coerce others into Hinduism. Canada has
neither state religion nor an anti-establishment restriction.

[
117
]

What the
Canadian Charter
,
the
United
Nations Covenant
and the
European Convention
have in common is a
guarantee that no person shall be subjected to oppression or repression on
religious grounds, or be compelled to conform to religious cult, doctrine or
belief. The
Lord's Day Act
does not offend that guarantee.

[
118
]

To the second question stated I would answer
that the
Lord's Day Act
does not infringe upon the freedom of religion
guaranteed in
s.2(a)
of the
Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms.

[
119
]

Having reached that conclusion on the second
question, it becomes unnecessary for me to answer the third question stated.
